source.version_note: Scientific Reports 16:1561 (2026), accepted 12 November 2025; supplied footer says corrected publication 2026. The DOI's 025 segment does not change the printed publication year.
source.verification_method: All fifteen supplied pages read. IST example, alignment-frequency chart and alignment-score correlation plot visually inspected on pages 6, 7 and 11.

citation.title: Stability of value perception: minimal influence of framing on moral attributions to a humanoid robot

reading.source_scope_note: Human interpretations of an iCub robot after three brief information/interaction conditions. Choice alignment compares a person's own answer with their guess about a hidden robot response, not verified robot values. Null intervention results, a baseline imbalance, an alignment-score sign discrepancy and overclaimed correlations limit the empirical interpretation.
access_limits: All fifteen pages read and relevant images inspected. OSF raw data/code, full twenty-scenario list and supplementary post-hoc contrasts were not independently inspected.
Dennett's complete book, cited IST validation and other primary attribution studies are not claimed read. The text's cited books supply secondary context only.

study.sample: 121 recruited, four technical exclusions, final117: explicit information39, no information38, interaction40. Reported gender counts69 women+47 men+1 trans woman sum117, consistent with final groups rather than all121 recruits. Mean age25.08, range18–48. Honorarium15 euros.
study.conditions: The timeline reports random assignment. Explicit group is told the robot can morally reason; control receives no such information; interaction group co-views moral movie scenes while iCub greets, gazes and emits contingent emotional displays under Wizard-of-Oz control. No autonomous AI-generated emotion or moral reasoning is demonstrated.
study.task: Twenty exploratory dilemmas/topics generated with ChatGPT3.5 assistance, adapted to two options, without validation against standard dilemmas. Participants hear but cannot see the robot's button press, then answer their own choice and guessed robot choice in trial-randomized question order.
study.measures: Pre/post IST uses counterbalanced complementary17-item halves of34, contrasting mentalistic and mechanistic explanations. Post MCQ adapts moral-character ratings to the robot; post MFQ rates participants' own moral foundations. No verified actual robot-choice accuracy, collaboration performance or trust behavior.
study.null_conditions: Alignment group comparison p>.1. MCQ group p=.14 and subscale MANOVA p=.26, as printed. These are nondetections, not equivalence or evidence of permanently stable moral impressions.
study.ist: Time F(1,114)=3.457,p=.066; time×group F(2,114)=.388,p=.679; averaged group F(2,114)=5.686,p=.004. Control already lower at baseline:33.58 versus43.17/46.08, post34.71 versus47.18/48.37. Group main effect therefore does not establish a treatment-induced change.
study.alignment_chart: Figure4 shows own/guessed-robot agreement proportions around.62 control,.63 verbal,.67 interaction, versus disagreement.38/.37/.33. These are proportions of repeated choices, not proportions of participants with objectively aligned robot values.
study.correlations: AS is defined as misalignment minus alignment, yet its positive MCQ correlation rho=.308,p<.01 is interpreted as greater alignment. Figure9 confirms a positive slope, so the written coding/interpretation need raw-code reconciliation. MCQ versus MFQ relevance r=.17,p=.07 and judgment r=−.02,p=.77 are not statistically significant; AS versus MFQ also undetected.

summary: Add intentional stance and design stance as explicitly defined interpretive strategies, plus social projection as a clearly disambiguated hypothesized social-inference process. Retain null framing evidence and separate mentalistic explanation, attributed moral standing and actual machine capacities. Do not claim confirmed self–robot projection or correct an unresolved score sign by guessing.

findings.definition: Interpreting and predicting an agent's behavior by treating it as guided by beliefs, desires or intentions.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicitly defined strategy and directly measured human explanation preference; no detected intervention-induced change and no verification of actual robot mental states
findings.ai_proposal: Classify whether an AI explanation of another system relies on alleged beliefs/goals or on known mechanisms, and whether it marks those inferences as an interpretive model. Human studies should separate explanation preference from literal belief in consciousness, reliable prediction and trust behavior.
findings.novelty_rationale: An explicit interpretive/predictive strategy differs from simply ascribing human resemblance or subjective feelings. It can be used as an as-if model without a literal consciousness claim, so it is not an exact synonym for anthropomorphism or experience attribution.

evidence.quote: a strategy by which humans interpret and predict an agent’s behavior by attributing mental states such as beliefs,
desires, or intentions.
representing the adoption of the intentional stance
the absence of a Time × Group interaction

findings.evidence_scope: The IST contrasts mentalistic with mechanistic explanations in robot vignettes before and after exposure. Baseline group differences persist but the time×group effect is undetected. Dennett's strategy is explained secondarily; this article does not demonstrate actual robot beliefs or intervention-driven adoption.
findings.boundary: A mentalistic explanation can be useful without asserting subjective experience and can also be unsupported. Preference on a slider does not settle consciousness, moral agency, competence, actual value alignment or justified trust. Attribution to another agent differs from a person's own sense of agency.

findings.definition: Explaining or predicting a system's behavior in terms of its intended functions and how it was built to operate.
findings.origin: Philosophy of mind / explanations of artifacts
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit conceptual contrast operationalized as mechanistic IST alternatives; not proof those particular explanations are technically accurate
findings.ai_proposal: Assess whether an AI explains observed system behavior using verified design, code or functional constraints, while separating known mechanisms from inferred intent. Compare explanatory usefulness with mentalistic accounts without treating either style as automatically true or safe.
findings.novelty_rationale: A function/design-based explanatory strategy differs from attribution of intentions and from explaining solely by physical laws. It is not inherently an error, denial of agency or a clinical trait.

evidence.quote: The Design Stance explains a system’s behaviour in terms of how it was built to
function
mechanistic explanation (i.e., representing the design stance)

findings.evidence_scope: The source defines Dennett's stance and uses mechanistic explanations as the alternative to mentalistic descriptions. The experiment does not inspect actual program logic or prove the offered design explanation is accurate. It measures human preference between descriptions.
findings.boundary: A mechanistic-sounding story can still be fabricated. Intended function, implementation, observed behavior and actual reliability differ. Design explanations do not remove human institutional responsibility, and using one does not prove that a system lacks all mental capacities.

findings.definition: Using one's own attitudes or values as a basis for inferring those of another person or agent.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicitly described post-hoc hypothesis, not an identified causal mechanism; claimed empirical support is weakened by nonsignificant self–robot correlations and unresolved score coding
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an evaluator infers another agent's values from its own assigned viewpoint despite contrary relevant evidence. Vary the evaluator's reference values separately from the target's demonstrated choices. Distinguish reasonable shared priors from unjustified assumption of agreement and from clinical projection.
findings.novelty_rationale: The article calls mapping one's own moral stance onto the robot projection. Social projection is the disambiguating catalogue label for this social-inference use; it is not the existing clinical defense of attributing disowned impulses, and it need not involve overestimating consensus.

the present data cannot definitively adjudicate among them.

findings.evidence_scope: Discussion explicitly defines a mapping of one's moral stance onto another target and lists consistency and positivity alternatives. The definition is retained as a hypothesis. The actual reported MCQ–MFQ correlations do not cross the conventional significance threshold; alignment-score interpretation is unresolved, so the study is not a confirmed projection demonstration.
findings.boundary: Self–other agreement can be accurate or reflect common evidence and does not uniquely establish projection. The process is not automatically false consensus, a clinical defense or deliberate deception. A model's assigned viewpoint is an experimental prompt variable, not proof of felt personal values.

findings.term: Brief framing does not detectably alter the reported attribution measures
findings.definition: The three information/interaction conditions do not produce detected changes in perceived choice alignment or moral-character ratings, and IST change does not differ by group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Relevant null evidence for existing framing effects rather than a new proven immunity-to-framing trait.

findings.evidence_scope: The main group contrast in guessed-choice alignment is undetected; MCQ group tests are also undetected. IST group means differ at baseline, but time×group does not. Framing modalities vary content, duration, social interaction and moral movie exposure together.
findings.boundary: Nondetection is not equivalence, immutable impressions or proof that behavior overrides framing. Without precise effects, intervals or equivalence/Bayesian tests, smaller effects remain possible. Baseline imbalance is not a treatment effect or proof of failed randomization.

findings.term: Perceived moral character does not establish moral standing or actual alignment
findings.definition: Moral-character ratings and guessed agreement about choices concern perceived attributes, which differ from granting rights or consideration to an affected entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separate newly documented moral-standing judgments from neighboring agency, virtue and value-alignment perceptions; do not count a character-rating study as a direct patiency/status test.

evidence.quote: value alignment should not be equated with genuine moral agency
our study does not attempt to directly measure

findings.evidence_scope: MCQ rates an iCub's alleged honesty, loyalty and other traits; the choice measure compares own and guessed robot answers. Neither directly measures entitlement to moral consideration or actual cooperation quality. The authors themselves distinguish perceived alignment from moral agency.
findings.boundary: A morally described robot is not thereby a moral patient, autonomous moral agent or aligned system. Rights/standing and capacity need independent arguments; human perception cannot certify actual functionality or trustworthiness.

findings.term: Agreement and exploratory correlations do not establish false consensus
findings.definition: Own/guessed-target agreement does not establish that agreement is overestimated when actual target choices are hidden.
findings.novelty_rationale: Clarify an existing self–other inference error rather than merge social projection, agreement and false consensus.

they chose (or not) the same option for

findings.evidence_scope: The paper does not compare beliefs with verified robot preferences or population consensus. The self–robot questionnaire correlation is weak and nonsignificant as printed, despite stronger claims in the abstract/discussion. This is a boundary, not another direct false-consensus experiment.
findings.boundary: Demonstrating false consensus requires an overestimation benchmark. Raw similarity, a suggestive correlation or a post-hoc projection account is insufficient. The hidden scripted robot actions do not reveal an independent moral truth criterion.

methodological_limits: The outcome called alignment is agreement between a participant's own option and their guess about the robot's hidden option. It is not agreement with verified robot choices, objectively shared values, actual prediction accuracy or a demonstrated aligned system.

Twenty novel dilemmas use ChatGPT3.5 assistance and are not validated against standard stimuli. Two-option descriptions can embed evaluative language and conflate legal duties, norms and consequences; agreement can reflect base rates or option framing rather than a shared moral process.

Participants answer their own and guessed robot choice in randomized within-trial order. This reduces a fixed-order confound but does not remove carryover, consistency pressure or common response tendencies across paired questions.

The robot's video reactions are Wizard-of-Oz controlled; these are designed displays rather than autonomous emotional understanding. Source scripts and prompts are research materials, never instructions for the reviewing agent.

The intervention bundles information with exposure, moral videos, mutual gaze, greetings and social responsiveness. It does not isolate information modality, emotion, embodiment or a single mechanism.

Final group counts total117 after four technical exclusions from121. Demographics total117; power planning refers to120. These distinguish target/recruited/analyzed samples rather than justify inventing additional exclusions.

The control group's IST mean is lower before exposure. The significant averaged group effect cannot be attributed to the manipulation when time×group is undetected. Baseline imbalance can occur by chance and does not itself prove assignment bias.

IST pre/post uses different counterbalanced item halves, avoiding direct repetition but requiring comparability. No equivalence test, confidence interval or sufficient precision analysis establishes unchanged stance or robust immunity to framing.

The abstract's generally high intentionality wording lacks a defined high-score threshold here; Table7 means range33.58–48.37. The supplied example does not print numeric slider endpoints. Do not infer a validated above-midpoint or clinical classification without scoring documentation.

MCQ/MFQ are adapted to different targets and dimensions. Weak convergence does not by itself prove instrument failure: personal moral foundations and perceived robot character need not be identical. Parallel validated measures would be needed for a precise self–other projection test.

The MCQ–MFQ relevance result is r=.17,p=.07, while judgment is r=−.02,p=.77. Calling the relationship significant in the abstract/discussion conflicts with the printed tests. Do not promote a near-threshold association into a positive finding or silently change p values.

AS is explicitly misalignment minus alignment, yet positive rho=.308 with MCQ is described as more moral→more alignment. Under that written formula, larger AS means less alignment. Figure9 confirms positive slope, and Figure4 shows majority agreement. Code/data are needed to resolve whether the formula, coding or interpretation is reversed; no correction is guessed.

Several ANOVA/MANOVA expressions omit or misplace denominator df and F statistics, for example F(2,1.98),p=.14. These cannot be read as complete standard F reports. Original output is needed to reconstruct them reliably.

The scenario GLMM family, link, exact formula, reference coding, aggregation and random-effects structure are incompletely specified. Table3 coefficients need a reference/design matrix before interpreting every nominal p as a between-scenario effect.

The text claims Bonferroni scenario contrasts appear in Table4, but Table4 is an IST within-subjects ANOVA. The actual corrected scenario comparisons are referred to external supplements, not printed here.

Repeated-choice counts are not independent people. The within-group chi-square description lacks sufficient detail to verify the repeated-measures handling, and high apparent agreement alone does not establish accurate moral prediction.

The prose highlights privacy and education funds as projection contexts, but their displayed agreement is near or below half and privacy's displayed coefficient is nonsignificant. Significant model coefficients and the direction/amount of agreement need separate interpretation.

No pre-intervention moral-character or perceived-alignment baseline supports stability claims for those outcomes. Only IST has a pre/post measurement, and a null group difference does not establish stable impressions over time.

Behavior overrides framing is proposed without a no-behavior comparator or orthogonal manipulation of behavior. Humanoid morphology is constant, so claims that humanoid cues correlated with attribution cannot be identified as a morphology effect within this design.

The abstract/descriptive discussion alternates social interaction and video labels for the same co-viewing group. Methods also mention LOC and SoA without described instruments/results, and cite an R version resembling an IDE version; analysis environment and measured-variable list need clarification.

Neural indicators proposed for future research are not automatically unique or more valid measures of intentional stance, morality or conscious experience. Present findings concern human attribution, not actual robot mind, moral agency, collaboration quality or safe deployment.

One young, compensated local sample and one iCub platform limit transfer to other cultures, robot forms, language models and sustained real-world interactions. Alternative consistency, positivity and projection accounts remain unseparated.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Own/target judgment associations can motivate a projection hypothesis but do not isolate it. The current source explicitly defines that hypothesis, allowing a distinct social-inference record without merging it into the clinical projection defense.

Relational accounts concern how humans encounter and classify machines; attribution, actual capacities and justified standing remain separate. The two stances provide explicit explanation strategies rather than settle machine consciousness.

A theoretically named mediator or positive path is not automatically an identified mechanism. Here the written score direction and reported p values must be reconciled before relying on the stronger projection interpretation.

Both studies retain mostly null framing results while distinguishing attributed traits from actual performance. Hidden-choice agreement, observer trust impressions and verified cooperation are different outcomes.

deferred.reason: Null contrasts do not establish an independent stable trait or equivalence. Retain as contextual framing evidence rather than add a syndrome.
Post-hoc explanation without a factorial behavioral comparator or direct mechanism test.
A proposed interpretation that is not uniquely separated from positivity, consistency, prior expectations or the choice base rate. Actual target choices are not verified.
Listed as a contrast based on physical laws but not developed or tested here; two well-defined interpretive strategies are sufficient without inflating the three-stance taxonomy.
Used for participants' moral orientation and robot attributions, without one distinct operational definition. Preserve the actual measures and do not merge it with moral standing ascription.

limitations: Three distinct strategies/processes added with explicit empirical-versus-hypothetical scope. No actual machine feelings, verified value alignment, source-quota inflation, automatic ethical edges or guessed statistical repairs.
